abstract: DNase I is a ubiquitous reagent, used to remove contaminating DNA from RNA preparations and other samples, and preparations from different suppliers are widely treated as interchangeable. Suppliers describe their products as improved --- faster, more complete, more stable --- but what better means is rarely defined in terms a user can reproduce: activity units are tied to each supplier's own assay, recommended protocols specify a single amount and a single time, and stability in storage, through freeze--thaw cycles and at working temperature, is seldom quantified. Here we adapt a low-cost fluorophore--quencher reporter of the kind used for Cas12 trans-cleavage diagnostics as a kinetic assay for DNase I, and compare preparations from three suppliers, each used at 1 U/ L, on plates that carry blanks, replicates and a standard of fully digested reporter. At large amounts (16--32 U) ThermoFisher and Zymo preparations were indistinguishable early in the reaction. At sub-saturating amounts ([≤]4 U) the product formed per labelled unit differed up to {approx}3.6-fold at 1 U (Zymo over ThermoFisher) and by considerably more at 0.25--0.5 U, where ThermoFisher signal was close to background. The ranking depended on dose, on time, and on whether rate or yield was the metric: from about 3 h onward ThermoFisher formed the least product at 1--4 U yet had the shortest fitted time constants, Synthego and Zymo were similar at [≤]1 U, and Synthego, slower to start, yielded more than Zymo after about 2--3 h at 4 U. On a single plate, two Zymo DNase I aliquots from different laboratories differed up to 19-fold at equal nominal volume. We argue that DNase I performance should be reported as calibrated dose--response and time-course data under stated conditions, with storage stability quantified, and that laboratories should verify the enzyme they actually hold. The reporter costs about $0.10 per reaction, is in principle readable on a simple LED fluorometer, and can be modified to probe dsDNA, RNA and nucleic-acid--binding proteins.
